primary_text_note: No text file supplied. Pre-1900 poems verified against Wikisource / americanliterature.com full texts; in-copyright poems verified against reputable study sources and the poets' publishers.

findings.claim: “Ozy” derives from the Greek ozium meaning “to breathe” or “air,” and “mandias” from mandate meaning “to rule.”
findings.truth: Invented etymology. Ozymandias is the Greek rendering of Ramesses II's throne name User-maat-Re (Usermaatre Setepenre), 'the justice of Ra is powerful'. 'Mandate' is Latin, not Greek.

findings.claim: He wrote “Ozymandias” in 1818 after hearing that archaeologists had discovered pieces of a funeral statue...
findings.truth: Shelley wrote the sonnet in December 1817; it was published on 11 January 1818 in The Examiner under the pen name Glirastes.

findings.claim: Card 4: a=“Percy”, q=“_____ Bysshe Shelley — Context Percy Bysshe Shelley (1792–1822) was one of the leading Romantic poets”
findings.truth: Broken cloze scraped from a heading. The answer word 'Percy' appears inside its own question, so the card cannot test anything.

findings.claim: Card 5: q=“He wrote “Ozymandias” in _____ after hearing...”, a=“1818”
findings.truth: Cloze fragment, and it also carried the wrong composition date. Reworded as a When question about publication, which 1818 answers correctly.

findings.claim: The verb “shattered” implies... / mark scheme: “Identifies 'shattered' as a violent verb”
findings.truth: In 'a shattered visage' the past participle modifies the noun, so it is an adjective. Naming the word class wrongly costs precision on the methods objective.
findings.evidence: Shelley, Ozymandias l.4: 'Half sunk a shattered visage lies'

findings.claim: oxymoron defined as “Placing two contrasting ideas, images or words together for effect.” (dfn, glossary and flashcard)
findings.truth: That is the definition of juxtaposition. An oxymoron is a single phrase made of two contradictory words, such as 'Marriage hearse'.
findings.evidence: Standard literary terminology; the lesson applies the term correctly to 'Marriage hearse' but defines it wrongly.

findings.claim: “Appalls” literally means “to make pale” (from the white funeral cloth)
findings.truth: 'Appal' comes from Old French apalir, to grow pale (Latin pallere). The funeral 'pall' is a separate word from Latin pallium, and a pall is not white. The pun on 'pall' is a reading, not an etymology.
findings.evidence: OED etymology of appal and pall

findings.claim: Cards 4 and 5 are heading fragments: “_____ — William Blake Context William Blake (1757–1827)...” and ““London” was published in his _____ collection Songs of Experience”
findings.truth: Broken clozes. Rewritten as Which / When questions with the same answers (London, 1794), both verified correct.

findings.claim: A league is about three miles, so half a league is roughly 1.7 miles
findings.truth: Half of three miles is 1.5 miles. The sentence contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: Arithmetic; a league is three statute miles.

findings.claim: Cards 4 and 5 both have the answer “Charge”, from two heading fragments
findings.truth: Duplicate answers inside one deck make both cards untestable (interference). Replaced with a poem-title card and a date card, answers now unique.
findings.evidence: docs/FLASHCARD_RULES.md rule 4; Tennyson wrote the poem on 2 December 1854.

findings.claim: patriotic = “The courage and willingness to sacrifice for one's country or a cause.” (dfn, glossary and flashcard)
findings.truth: Patriotic means showing loyalty to and pride in your country. The definition given describes valour, and it makes the lesson's own phrase 'patriotic courage' circular.
findings.evidence: Standard definition; the same lesson defines 'patriotism' correctly.

findings.claim: Lucrezia de' Medici, who died in 1561 aged just 17, only two years after their marriage
findings.truth: Born 14 February 1545, married Alfonso II on 3 July 1558, died 21 April 1561. She was 16, and the marriage had lasted nearly three years.

findings.claim: Card 5: a=“Duchessrdquo”
findings.truth: Mangled HTML entity (rdquo) left in the answer, so the card teaches a non-word. Rebuilt as a Which question answered 'My Last Duchess'.

findings.claim: Card 4: a=“Robert”, q=“_____ Browning — Context Robert Browning (1812–1889)...”
findings.truth: Broken cloze whose answer sits inside its own question.

findings.claim: The first eight letters of “Stormont” ... are hidden in the title: STORMonTheIsland
findings.truth: The claim is back to front: the first eight letters of the TITLE spell Stormont (Storm on t...). The markup also bolded STORM, T and I, which spells nothing.
findings.evidence: Title 'Storm on the Island'; Stormont is eight letters, so 'the first eight letters of Stormont' is the whole word.

findings.claim: the poem can also be read as an allegory for the political conflict in Northern Ireland (the Troubles), where communities lived under constant threat of violence
findings.truth: The allegorical reading is standard and stays, but the poem was published in Death of a Naturalist in 1966, before the Troubles began in the late 1960s. The date is now stated so students do not claim Heaney wrote about a conflict that had not started.
findings.evidence: Death of a Naturalist, Faber, May 1966; the Troubles are dated from 1968-69.

findings.claim: Card 5: a=“1917ndash18”
findings.truth: Mangled HTML entity (ndash) in the answer. Rebuilt as a When question with the answer 1917–18.

findings.claim: Card 4: q=“_____ — Wilfred Owen Context Wilfred Owen (1893–1918)...”
findings.truth: Broken cloze fragment; rewritten as a Which question with the same answer.

findings.claim: 30-mark mark scheme ladder labels both 25-30 and 13-18 as “Top band”
findings.truth: Two different bands carried the same name. Re-laddered to the house names: Top / Upper-mid / Mid / Lower-mid / Low / Basic.

findings.claim: Same duplicated “Top band” ladder on the 30-mark question
findings.truth: Re-laddered to the house band names.

findings.claim: Match item quotes Tissue as “raised a structure never meant to last”
findings.truth: The poem reads 'raise a structure / never meant to last'. The tense was wrong in a quotation students are asked to match.

findings.claim: Card 4: a=“Tissue”, q=“_____ — Imtiaz Dharker Imtiaz Dharker wrote Tissue as part of her 2006 collection...”
findings.truth: Broken cloze whose answer appears inside its own question.

findings.claim: Same duplicated “Top band” ladder on the 30-mark question
findings.truth: Re-laddered to the house band names.

findings.claim: Jane Weir described as “A Manchester-based poet”
findings.truth: Weir was born in Manchester in 1963 but lives in Derbyshire. The lesson's more useful context (she is a textile designer) is correct. Not worth an edit on its own.

findings.claim: “a huge peak, black and huge, as if with voluntary purpose” — quoted twice in the content and used as the whole subject of practice question 1 and its mark scheme
findings.truth: The line reads 'a huge peak, black and huge, / As if with voluntary power instinct, / Upreared its head'. 'Voluntary purpose' is not in the poem; 'with purpose of its own' is a different line three lines later.

findings.claim: “No familiar shapes remained, no pleasant images of trees, of sea, or sky, no colours of green, or blue, or silver.”
findings.truth: The poem reads 'no colours of green fields'. The 'green, or blue, or silver' list is fabricated.

findings.claim: The extract studied for AQA Power and Conflict comes from Book One of The Prelude (1799 version)
findings.truth: Two faults. The exam board is named in student-facing text, and the anthology extract is the Book One text of the later Prelude; the 1799 poem is in two Parts, not Books.
findings.evidence: Wordsworth, The Prelude (1805/1850) Book First; the two-part Prelude of 1799 has no 'Book One'.

findings.claim: Same duplicated “Top band” ladder on the 30-mark question
findings.truth: Re-laddered to the house band names.

findings.claim: “The 30 marks are split across four Assessment Objectives: AO1..., AO2..., AO3..., and AO4 (comparison — similarities and differences between the two poems)”, repeated in the revision tip, the SEAS section, the conclusion, two practice questions, the glossary, and a knowledge check whose key marks 'Comparison of the two poems' as the meaning of AO4.
findings.truth: AO4 is 'use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures for clarity, purpose and effect, with accurate spelling and punctuation'. The anthology comparison is 30 marks split AO1 12 / AO2 12 / AO3 6, with no AO4 or SPaG marks at all. Comparison is credited inside AO1 and AO2. The knowledge check was marking a false statement correct, so it is re-pointed at AO3 with the key moved to 'Contextual knowledge'.
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/english-literature-8702-8702.md section 4.2; board facts for Paper 2 Section B (30 marks, AO1 12 / AO2 12 / AO3 6, no SPaG). Lessons 1-5 of this unit state the correct 12/12/6 split.

findings.claim: “The Paper 2 Section B Question”, “In the AQA English Literature exam, Paper 2 Section B gives you...”, “Why does AQA reward comparison...” (4 x paper/section code, 3 x board name across content, conclusion, practice and a knowledge check)
findings.truth: House rule: never name the exam board in student-facing text, and paper/section codes are banned strings. Replaced with 'the poetry anthology section' and 'examiners'. Lesson 9 carried one further board name (see F27); no other lesson names the board.

findings.claim: Same duplicated “Top band” ladder on the 30-mark question
findings.truth: Re-laddered to the house band names.

findings.claim: Lesson descriptions run over the 100-character limit: L6 101, L8 113, L9 120, L10 105 characters.
findings.truth: A validator limit, not a factual error, so left alone. Worth a trim if the unit is ever revalidated.
findings.evidence: raw/L06.txt, L08, L09, L10 DESCRIPTION blocks

findings.claim: Blake quoted as “I wander through each charter'd street”
findings.truth: Blake wrote 'I wander thro' each charter'd street'. The lesson silently modernises the spelling. No marks are at risk, so it is left as it stands.

findings.claim: Every lesson offers practice questions labelled “4 marks — Quote Analysis”, “8 marks — Extract Analysis” and “12 marks — Extended Response” alongside the real 30-mark comparison.
findings.truth: This section of the paper has exactly one question, worth 30 marks; no 4, 8 or 12-mark poetry question exists. The labels are house practice scaffolding rather than a claim about the paper, and the same pattern runs across every article unit on the platform. Options: (a) leave, and treat the labels as practice tiers, which is my recommendation because a change here alone would make this unit inconsistent with the rest of the fleet; (b) relabel fleet-wide to 'Practice: 4 marks' style so no student reads them as exam questions.
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/english-literature-8702-8702.md section 2 (Paper 2 Section B: one comparative question)

summary: All ten lessons carried at least one finding: 6 HIGH (two fabricated Prelude quotations; the AO4-is-comparison error running through the whole exam-skills lesson, including a knowledge check that marked a false answer correct; three decks with a mangled-entity or duplicated flashcard answer), 13 MEDIUM and 15 LOW. 30 findings produced 61 surgical edits in _edits.json, dry-run clean against the raw rows; one ADJUDICATE (platform-wide practice-question mark labels) and three NOTEs are left unedited.
